lines.say: A typical US home costs nearly five years of income.

lines.text: In the 1990s, it was closer to three. So what happened?
lines.say: In the nineteen nineties, it was closer to three. So what happened?

lines.text: The median existing home sold for $223,900 in 2015, and $414,400 in 2025.
lines.say: The median existing home sold for about two hundred twenty-four thousand dollars in twenty fifteen, and about four hundred fourteen thousand in twenty twenty-five.
The biggest jump: twenty twenty-one, up nineteen percent.

lines.text: Reason one: not enough homes. Freddie Mac estimated a shortage of about 3.7 million in 2024.
lines.say: Reason one: not enough homes. Freddie Mac estimated a shortage of about three point seven million in twenty twenty-four.

lines.text: Reason two: rates. The average 30-year mortgage rate hit 7.03% in late September 2026.
lines.say: Reason two: rates. The average thirty-year mortgage rate hit seven point oh three percent in late September twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: With 10% down on August's $429,100 median, that's about $2,577 a month, versus $1,628 at 3%.
lines.say: With ten percent down on August's median, that's about twenty-five seventy-seven a month, versus sixteen twenty-eight at three percent.

lines.text: Reason three: lock-in. Owners with cheap old mortgages stay put, so fewer homes get listed.
lines.say: Reason three: lock-in. Owners with cheap old mortgages stay put, so fewer homes get listed.

lines.text: Too few homes, high rates, and few sellers stack up. That's the wall buyers hit.

post.title: Why a typical home now costs nearly 5 years of income
post.ig:
A typical US home costs nearly five years of income.
Harvard JCHS: price-to-income was 4.7 in 2025, vs about 3.2 in the 1990s.
NAR median existing-home price: $223,900 in 2015, $414,400 in 2025, $429,100 in Aug 2026.
Why: a shortage Freddie Mac put at ~3.7M homes (2024), 30-year rates at 7.03% (Sept 24, 2026), and owners locked into cheap old mortgages.
Example: $386,190 loan = ~$2,577/mo at 7.03% vs ~$1,628 at 3%.
Sources: Harvard JCHS 2026; NAR; Freddie Mac.
